category: "guide"

# Set up a shared Alexa+ household whiteboard for the whole family

> **In short:** With Alexa+, you create one named list (think of it as a shared whiteboard) that every adult in the household can add to by speaking to any Echo in the house, and read back the same way. Setup takes about five minutes; using it is one sentence per note.

You can already talk to Alexa to add items to a shopping list — this guide turns that same idea into a wall everyone in the family actually reads. Think of it as a fridge notepad that updates itself whenever anyone speaks. A partner can drop a note on the kitchen Echo while you're at the grocery store, and you'll hear it when you walk in the door.

> **Before you start**
> - You already use Alexa on at least one Echo device in your home (you've added items to a list or asked a question out loud). You also have the Alexa app installed on your phone and you're signed in with your Amazon account.
> - You need **two or more adult profiles linked to the same Amazon Household** in the Alexa app — that's how everyone in the family gets permission to write to the same board. If you live alone, you can still use the guide, but the "shared" benefit only kicks in once a second adult is added to the Household.
> - **Time needed:** about 5 minutes for setup, then a few seconds per note from then on.
> - **Cost:** this works on the standard Alexa experience; Alexa+ features are rolling out gradually and may require an Alexa+ subscription on some accounts. If a step below gives you an "upgrade" prompt, that is what it is — you can still use a basic named list without Alexa+.

---

## Step 1 — Open the Alexa app and find Household settings
On your phone, open the **Alexa app** (the orange speech-bubble icon — if you can't find it, search your home screen for "Alexa"). Tap the **Devices** tab along the bottom — it usually looks like a small house or plug icon. At the top-right of the Devices screen, tap the **Settings** gear icon (look for it if your layout differs, sometimes it's behind a **⋯** menu). Scroll down until you see a section called **Your Household** or **Amazon Household**.

**What happens next:** A list of adults and children linked to your Amazon account appears. If more than one adult is already listed, you're set up. If you're the only adult, you'll need to invite someone (a partner, a grown child) before shared notes will reach them.

💬 Example: say to yourself *"I want everyone in the house to be able to read this board."* That's the goal — the next steps get you there.

**You'll know it worked when** you see at least two adult names (yours plus one other) listed under Your Household, or you successfully sent an invite that the other person accepted.

## Step 2 — Create a dedicated list for the whiteboard
Back on the main screen of the Alexa app, tap the **Communicate** or **Lists** icon (it depends on your app version — look for a checklist or speech-bubble-with-lines icon at the bottom, often labeled **Lists**, **Notes**, or **More**). Inside the Lists area, look for a button or link that says **Create List** (sometimes hidden behind a **+** plus-sign icon). Name the list something everyone will recognize — for example: *Family Board*, *House Notes*, or *Fridge Board*.

**What happens next:** A new named list appears in your Lists tab. This list is the "whiteboard." Anything spoken into any Echo in your home and added to this list will show up here, and any adult in the Household can read it.

💬 Example: name it `Family Board` — short, obvious, and easy to remember when you say it out loud.

**You'll know it worked when** the new list shows up in the Lists tab and Alexa confirms the name when you ask her (try: *"Alexa, what's on Family Board?"* — she should say the list is empty).

## Step 3 — Add your first note by voice
Stand within earshot of any Echo in your home and say the wake word — usually **"Alexa,"** but yours might be **"Echo,"** **"Amazon,"** or **"Computer,"** depending on what you picked during setup. Then speak a single sentence that includes the list name and what you want to add. Speak naturally, at a normal pace — you don't need to pause between words.

**What happens next:** Alexa chimes or flashes a blue ring (on older Echos) or a blue light bar (on newer ones), then repeats your note back and confirms it was added to the list. Open the Alexa app's Lists tab to see the note appear as text within a few seconds.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, add 'Pick up dry cleaning on the way home' to Family Board."*

**You'll know it worked when** Alexa repeats the note back to you AND it shows up in the Family Board list inside the app. If only one of those two things happens, see Common mistakes below.

## Step 4 — Have another household member post their own note
This is the moment that turns a personal list into a shared board. Ask the other adult in your Amazon Household to walk up to a different Echo (a different room is the whole point) and speak a note the same way you did. They use their own voice, and they don't need to open the app at all — they just talk to the Echo.

**What happens next:** That note lands on the same Family Board list inside your Alexa app, alongside yours. Both of you can read every note, no matter which Echo it was spoken to.

💬 Example: your partner says, *"Alexa, add 'Sam has soccer practice at 4' to Family Board."* You see it on your phone within a few seconds.

**You'll know it worked when** a note spoken in one room appears in the Family Board list in the Alexa app on another adult's phone. If it doesn't, double-check that the other person is listed as an adult in the Amazon Household (Step 1).

## Step 5 — Read the board back out loud from any Echo
The board isn't just for writing — it's also for reading hands-free. From any Echo in the house, ask Alexa to read the list back to you. Useful moments: while cooking, while getting the kids ready, while walking in the door. You can also ask how many items are on it without hearing them all.

**What happens next:** Alexa reads each note out loud in the order they were added. For a long board, she'll usually say something like *"You have seven items"* first, then ask if you want to hear them all.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, what's on Family Board?"* — full readout. *"Alexa, how many items are on Family Board?"* — just the count.

**You'll know it worked when** Alexa reads your notes back without you opening the app.

## Step 6 — Pin the routine and tell the family how to use it
A whiteboard only helps if people remember to use it. Take two minutes to tell the family how it works: "Say *Alexa, add [your note] to Family Board* from any Echo in the house. Ask *Alexa, what's on Family Board?* to hear the notes." If you have a wall Echo or Echo Show, you can also enable the Alexa app's list screen on the Show so notes scroll visibly in the kitchen.

**What happens next:** Over the next few days, the board fills up with the small things people would otherwise forget to mention — reminders, asks, wins. Old notes stay on the list until you delete them.

💬 Example: a shared line the family can memorize: *"Alexa, add [thing] to Family Board."*

**You'll know it worked when** notes start appearing without anyone asking *"did you see my message?"* — the board becomes the answer.

---

## Common mistakes
- **"Alexa added it to Shopping List, not Family Board."** You forgot to say the list name. Every voice note has to end with *"to Family Board"* (or whatever you named it). Fix: delete the wrong entry in the app and re-speak the note with the list name at the end.
- **"My partner's notes don't show up in my app."** They probably aren't listed as an adult in your Amazon Household. Fix: go back to Step 1 and either add them as an adult or have them accept the Household invite on their own account.
- **"Alexa says she can't find the list."** The list name has to match exactly what you said — *"Family Board"* and *"Family Boards"* are different to Alexa. Fix: pick a short, one-or-two-word name in Step 2 and stick with it.

---

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Less "did you tell me about…?" and fewer missed dentist appointments. The board works because speaking a note takes one second and reading it back takes even less — nobody has to remember to open an app.
- **For your business or work:** This same trick works for a home office: create a list called *"Work Notes"* and use it as a quick voice-captured idea log. Speak thoughts while doing dishes, review them at your desk later.
- **If you want to go further:** Try a second list for time-sensitive things — *"Errands Today"* — and delete items off it each evening as a simple habit. Two short lists are easier to scan than one long one, and the daily reset keeps the board from turning into a junk drawer.

---

## Try it now
Pick one note that's on your mind right now — a reminder, an errand, something you keep forgetting to mention. Stand near any Echo and say: *"Alexa, add [your note] to Family Board."* That's it. You now have a household whiteboard, and the family can start posting to it tonight.
